    14	# Endurance Athletes Need Specialised Strength and Jump Work: The Authors' 800 m Benchmarks
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors argue that "the importance of muscular adaptation to intense and prolonged work invariably is underestimated" and that "specialisation of the muscles, as the direct executor of the work, is of greater significance than development of the cardiovascular-respiratory component of endurance. A more intense stimulus is necessary for promoting adaptation of the muscles to endurance work than for producing cardiovascular and respiratory conditioning." Long-duration work alone can leave "a definite imbalance" between cardiorespiratory function and "the working potential of the muscles," and then "the anticipated sporting proficiency will not result" (PDF pp. 367-368 / printed pp. 356-357, checked against the page images). Their illustration: "This situation is very typical of the preparation of middle-distance runners. Elementary logic decrees that in order to run 800m in 1:45:0, it is necessary to be able to achieve a time of 10.6-10.7 seconds in the 100m. One needs to possess great strength potential to do this, e.g. the ability to execute three consecutive standing long jumps covering a total distance of at least 9m, or ten consecutive standing long jumps totalling 33-34m, for which middle-distance runners usually do not have the strength" (PDF p. 368). The remedy: "specialised strength and jump training which exerts a stronger influence on the muscles than distance training," raising local muscular endurance including "'anaerobic' energy production," so that "it is possible to reduce the volume of exhausting endurance work in the 'anaerobic' glycolytic zone (Zhdanovich, 1980; Verkhoshansky & Sirenko, 1982)" (same page). Such work should "firstly increase strength up to a definite optimum, and secondly, exploit the specific energy processes crucial for producing repeated motor actions"; "The main thing is to overcome the archaic viewpoint which regards strength training as a means of increasing absolute strength alone" (same page). Earlier, in italics: "It is undoubtedly important to increase strength, but this is not the fundamental and sole task of strength training" (PDF p. 367).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism: strength and jump work loads the muscles harder than distance running, "thereby intensifying their adaptation to endurance work and activating the relevant functional reserves," enhancing "the power and the capacity of the metabolic processes" (PDF p. 368).
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — Endurance or mixed-demand athletes whose conditioning is mostly long-duration running: add specialised strength and jump work aimed at repeated efforts, and expect to need less glycolytic volume. Eric's baseline: "For speed-power athletes, the aerobic system's main value is inter-effort recovery ... not distance capacity" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 123, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the authors make the converse point for endurance athletes, that strength and power support the endurance event; together they argue against treating strength and conditioning as separate silos, as does the baseline's "Everything we do is some form of conditioning" (line 122, Explicit).
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — The 800 m benchmarks are introduced as "Elementary logic decrees"; they are asserted, not measured, and no study links the jump distances to 800 m performance. The cited studies are named without data. Inference: the benchmarks are for elite men's 800 m (1:45.0) and say nothing about lower standards or women's events.
    23	
    24	**Example** — The authors' own: an 800 m runner aiming at 1:45.0 should, by their reasoning, be able to run 100 m in 10.6-10.7 s and cover at least 9 m in three consecutive standing long jumps or 33-34 m in ten, which "middle-distance runners usually do not have the strength" to do (PDF p. 368 / printed p. 357).
    25

    12	---
    13	
    14	# Volume Drives Long-Term Adaptation and Prepares Connective Tissue; Intensify Only After Extensive Low-Intensity Work
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors give volume two roles. First: "The function of the volume of the load consists chiefly of the systematic and prolonged disturbance of the body's homeostasis, which stimulates the mobilisation of its energy resources and plastic reserves. This is the fundamental condition for switching from the acute (specific) reaction ... to the general (non-specific) adaptive reaction, and then to the development of long-term adaptation of the body. Therefore, in each successive annual cycle athletes should execute larger volumes of loading (within optimal limits) to raise and maintain the special work-capacity" (PDF p. 369 / printed p. 358, checked against the page image). Second, in sports with "brief, highly concentrated efforts": "the mechanical integrity of the ligamentous-joint apparatus can become the limiting factor to the progress of sporting performance" (italics in the original). "If these connective tissues are not prepared by extensive work of moderate intensity, then the great dynamic overloading encountered at the level of peak performance can lead to severe joint injury. This occurs frequently in gymnastics, weightlifting, high jumping and triple jumping" (same page).
    17	
    18	Volume alone is not enough: "the influence of the volume can be determined correctly only if one also takes into consideration the magnitude of the loading, its duration and intensity" (PDF p. 369). Magnitude is set "first of all, on the basis of the athlete's qualification": the higher the qualification, the larger the yearly and stage volume, and the share of "specialised loading" grows (Panov 1975; Zhikharevich 1976; Vankov 1977; Matveyev 1977; Gilyazova 1978). The annual volume is "established individually" from the preceding stages; "A more serious task" is the optimal volume per month, stage or phase (same page). On intensity: it "determines the strength and specificity of its effect on the body," regulates "the training potential of the given means," frequency and intervals, and "the ratio of the volume of the loading divided by the time taken to reach the maximum load in a given stage," a measure of "loading concentration relative to time." "Intensification of loading is permitted during specific stages in the annual cycle and only after preliminary preparation with extensive low intensity loading (see Fig 6.1)" (PDF p. 370 / printed p. 359, checked against the page image).
    19	
    20	**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism is the one quoted: prolonged homeostatic disturbance mobilises "energy resources and plastic reserves" and moves the body from an acute to a general, then long-term, adaptive reaction (PDF p. 369). For connective tissue they refer back to 1.6 and 1.7.2 and give no further mechanism here.
    21	
    22	**When to apply** — Building a multi-year plan (raise annual volume, within limits, as qualification rises) and opening each year with extensive moderate-intensity work before intensifying, especially in jumping and other high-impact events. Eric's baseline: "Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design; abrupt, large changes are treated as a direct injury-risk driver" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 142, Inferred (transcript)). Eric's baseline: "The Vermeil hierarchy of athletic development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill ...)" (line 101, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Inference: the authors' "extensive low intensity loading" before intensification is close to the work-capacity base of that hierarchy.
    23	
    24	**When NOT to apply** — "within optimal limits" is not quantified, and the rule to raise volume every year cannot run indefinitely; the authors elsewhere set a limit by current adaptation reserves (PDF p. 370) and an optimum above which the LDTE pattern appears (PDF p. 374, [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]]). The joint-injury link is stated as frequent in four sports with no data. Inference: in American collegiate football, where many athletes are four- or five-year players, a rising-volume rule would need to be weighed against Eric's baseline that recovery is handled "through training-load design alone" (line 153, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q23)), since nothing else would catch an overshoot. The book's 4.1.2 passage gives volume two different functions (a functional base and endurance development; [[heuristic--structured-load-progression-beats-volume-alone-or-random-combination]]); Inference: the two lists overlap on the "base" role and differ on the second, so read them together rather than as rival definitions.
    25	
    26	**Example** — The authors' own: gymnastics, weightlifting, high jumping and triple jumping, where joint injury "occurs frequently" if connective tissue has not been prepared by extensive moderate-intensity work before peak dynamic loads (PDF p. 369 / printed p. 358). Inference: a jumper's year would open with weeks of moderate-volume, lower-impact jumping and strength work before depth jumps.
    27	
    28	**Related** — [[claim--time-limits-of-single-emphasis-loading-by-motor-quality]], [[heuristic--structured-load-progression-beats-volume-alone-or-random-combination]], [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]], [[claim--ligament-tendon-adaptation-and-detraining-response]], [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]], [[heuristic--preparatory-progression-before-depth-jumps]], [[framework--logical-scheme-of-training-management-load-fitness-state-external-interactions]] (6.4, training potential as relative to current fitness), [[heuristic--replace-means-as-their-training-effect-fades]], [[periodization--bompa/principle--progressive-overload-threshold]]

content.content:
**When NOT to apply** — The 1-3 week figure is "most commonly," with no study named. It is a latency to the onset of gains. Chapter 6 gives a different number for a different quantity: the long-term delayed training effect "was observed to last from 4-12 weeks during the long-term stages of strength preparation," its duration "approximately equal to the duration of the strength training stage," and its appearance "individualised" (PDF p. 375 / printed p. 364, checked against the page image). **Contested across the library:** Bompa & Haff (5th ed.), not Supertraining, write that "Siff and Verkhoshansky (83) suggested that performance gains may occur 4 to 12 weeks after the cessation of the concentrated loading phase" (Bompa & Haff 5e, PDF idx 60 / printed p. 49), and the Bompa entry [[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]] repeats this as a 4-12 week delay. Bompa & Haff also say that "the greater the magnitude and duration of the concentrated loading phase, the more time needed for fatigue to dissipate and performance to improve" (same page, refs 83, 91, 103, 104). Inference: read as a 4-12 week wait before gains, the Bompa & Haff sentence matches neither Supertraining statement: 5.3.3 gives a 1-3 week latency to gains (PDF p. 305 / printed p. 294), and Chapter 6 gives 4-12 weeks as how long the delayed effect lasts (PDF p. 375 / printed p. 364). Read as the window in which gains show, it is close to the Chapter 6 figure. Fig 6.31 on that page (checked against the page image) shows the timing: the trained qualities (F1-F3) are depressed during the concentrated loading stage T1 and climb during T2, which begins where T1 ends (dashed line). The other 4-12 week figures in the book are also durations: Chapter 6 calls unidirectional training "for prolonged stages (4-12 weeks)" very effective (PDF p. 381 / printed p. 370, text layer), and the Addendum says "the tendency has been for the stages to last anywhere from 4-12 weeks," with the delayed effect's duration "equal to the duration of the stage" (PDF p. 536 / printed p. 525, text layer). Use the onset figure for when to expect a result and the duration figure for how long it may hold. Chapter 6 also qualifies the warning: during the emergence of the delayed effect "it is relatively easy and painless for the body to change to intensive loading, but it will react negatively to extensive work" (PDF p. 375 / printed p. 364), so the restorative period is about volume, not a full stop.

lines: **What it is** — The authors argue that "the importance of muscular adaptation to intense and prolonged work invariably is underestimated" and that "specialisation of the muscles, as the direct executor of the work, is of greater significance than development of the cardiovascular-respiratory component of endurance. A more intense stimulus is necessary for promoting adaptation of the muscles to endurance work than for producing cardiovascular and respiratory conditioning." Long-duration work alone can leave "a definite imbalance" between cardiorespiratory function and "the working potential of the muscles," and then "the anticipated sporting proficiency will not result" (PDF pp. 367-368 / printed pp. 356-357, checked against the page images). Their illustration: "This situation is very typical of the preparation of middle-distance runners. Elementary logic decrees that in order to run 800m in 1:45:0, it is necessary to be able to achieve a time of 10.6-10.7 seconds in the 100m. One needs to possess great strength potential to do this, e.g. the ability to execute three consecutive standing long jumps covering a total distance of at least 9m, or ten consecutive standing long jumps totalling 33-34m, for which middle-distance runners usually do not have the strength" (PDF p. 368). The remedy: "specialised strength and jump training which exerts a stronger influence on the muscles than distance training," raising local muscular endurance including "'anaerobic' energy production," so that "it is possible to reduce the volume of exhausting endurance work in the 'anaerobic' glycolytic zone (Zhdanovich, 1980; Verkhoshansky & Sirenko, 1982)" (same page). Such work should "firstly increase strength up to a definite optimum, and secondly, exploit the specific energy processes crucial for producing repeated motor actions"; "The main thing is to overcome the archaic viewpoint which regards strength training as a means of increasing absolute strength alone" (same page). Earlier, in italics: "It is undoubtedly important to increase strength, but this is not the fundamental and sole task of strength training" (PDF p. 367).

+The argument grows out of the authors' rule for choosing SPP means (6.9.3, PDF p. 367 / printed p. 356, checked against the page image). "In practice the external similarity of the training means to the fundamental sport exercise is often overemphasized, whereas the importance of the similarity of the means to the regime of muscular work and to the mechanism of its energy production is underemphasized"; barbell squats "bear little resemblance" to running, throwing or basketball, but "the use of squats is justified." Then: "the need to preserve the training potential of the loading (especially for highly qualified athletes) requires using means that not only conform to, but exceed, competition conditions, with regard to maximum force, time of maximum force development and the power of the metabolic processes which determine work-capacity. On this basis, it is easy to conclude that satisfaction of this requirement should be associated with improving the strength component of the movement" (same page). Section 6.8.3 sets the same frame from the other side: "supplementary or 'cross' training cannot simply be used in a very general way," "muscle endurance gained through supplementary running training does not mean that it will directly improve the performance of a competitive rower or cyclist," and "The emergence of specificity from an array of non-specific fitness qualities, however, is not supported by current physiological and biochemical research" (PDF p. 363 / printed p. 352, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism: strength and jump work loads the muscles harder than distance running, "thereby intensifying their adaptation to endurance work and activating the relevant functional reserves," enhancing "the power and the capacity of the metabolic processes" (PDF p. 368).

# Fixes applied: Supertraining 6.8.3-6.11 (Ch6c), 19 entries

Fixer: Claude Opus. Date: 2026-10-03. Review: `staging/review_supertraining_ch6c_opus.md` (round 1, GO AFTER FIXES: 9 FIX rows, 9 numbered fixes, 3 missing ideas, reciprocal-link suggestions).
Source checked: `staging/books/supertraining-6th-expanded.pdf`. I extracted the text of PDF idx 288, 299-301, 305, 363, 365, 367-377, 514, 515 and 536 with PyMuPDF (`staging/_tmp/f6c_text.txt`). I rendered PDF 288, 299, 300, 301 (top crop), 305, 363, 365, 367-373, 375, 377, 515 (top crop) and 536 to `staging/_renders/f6c_p<N>.png`, plus 300 dpi crops of Fig 6.25 (`f6c_p365_fig625.png`) and Figs 6.30-6.31 (`f6c_p375_top.png`). I opened every one of those images. Not opened as images: PDF 374 and 376 (the sentences I cite from them are unchanged text), and the PDF 35/38 section headings (text layer only, labelled so in the entry). Page key: PDF idx = printed + 11.
Scope: the 19 files in `staging/_scope_supertraining_ch6c.txt`. I edited the 9 FIX entries plus 2 GO entries (`principle--loading-volume-disturbs-homeostasis-and-prepares-connective-tissue`, `claim--middle-distance-runners-need-strength-and-jump-training-benchmarks`) to place the missing ideas. No new entries, so the scope file is unchanged (19 lines). No renames. I did not edit `_book.md`, any 6b or 6d file, or the vault.

| file | what changed |
|---|---|
| principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum.md | **Fix 1.** (1) Fig 6.30 block now "from about month 1.6 to about month 4.5 (read from a 300 dpi render of the page image)". (2) When NOT adds the three 4-12 week referents: PDF 305 / p.294 (unidirectional training effective, checked against the page image), PDF 375 (LDTE duration), and "Verkhoshansky's Addendum paper (9.1, translated by Yessis; PDF p. 515)", quoting "the tendency has been for the stages to last anywhere from 4-12 weeks" (PDF 536 / p.525, checked against the page image). It says T2 about equal to T1, stated on both 375 and 536, reconciles those two, and PDF 305 is a separate quantity. "Keep the locator with the number." |
| heuristic--time-technique-and-competition-strength-work-to-the-ldte-window.md | **Fix 2.** (1) "The Addendum restates" is now "Verkhoshansky's Addendum paper (9.1, "Dr. Yuri Verkhoshansky, Translated from the Russian by Dr. Michael Yessis"; PDF p. 515 / printed p. 504, checked against the page image) restates". The Inference now reads: "its own example fits Chapter 6, and the Addendum is a separate translation of Verkhoshansky's text, which makes a translation slip plausible. The book prints both." The example quote in When NOT now quotes the page's own words ("insignificant increase ... (by only a few percent)") rather than "triple jumpers whose ... volume rose". (2) The Example is now "Verkhoshansky's own, from the Addendum". It quotes Figure 8 "in triple jumpers" and records that the page switches to the singular ("as believed by the athlete"; "the athlete lost his chance to be selected ... for a place on the national team"). (3) Related adds [[heuristic--technique-work-during-and-after-a-concentrated-strength-block]] (file confirmed present before linking). `contested` kept. |
| claim--ldte-in-endurance-training-documented-only-after-altitude-training.md | **Fix 3.** The Susman gloss is replaced with the review's wording: "The authors do not call this an LDTE; they give it after stating that disturbance of homeostasis 'can be detected in the dynamics of a number of psycho-physiological indicators' (PDF p. 377). Inference: it is offered as a sea-level example of the dip-and-rebound pattern in non-aerobic measures, not as a documented LDTE in aerobic productivity." |
| claim--concentrated-beats-distributed-loading-for-highly-qualified-athletes.md | **Fix 4.** (1) "Their conclusion, partly italicised in the original (only 'concentration of the volume of uni-directional loading produces more extensive functional changes and greater improvement' is in italics):". (2) Related adds [[framework--distributed-vs-concentrated-loading-two-forms-of-compensatory-adaptation]] and [[claim--complex-training-falls-short-for-highly-qualified-athletes]] (both confirmed present at 13:51). (3) Optional applied: "Inference: this is a disagreement about scope and evidence sufficiency; the sprinter and jumper studies fall outside the sports Issurin names." `contested` kept. |
| heuristic--within-session-order-of-explosive-means-matters-less-than-volume-and-contrast.md | **Fix 5.** The "Contested inside the book" paragraph is rewritten. PDF 371 is called "a hedge, not a contradiction". The cross-chapter conflict is laid out with locators, each checked against the page image: PDF 288 (resistance before plyometrics "in individual sessions"), PDF 299 (novices, "no statistically significant difference"), and PDF 300 ("Research with novices and athletes of average qualification": "Least effective is the sequence of strength followed by speed-strength means during the same session"). The opposition to p.371 is labelled Inference (see Disagreements 1). The PDF 301 bullets are moved out as stage-level, quoting the PDF 300 heading, with a pointer to the sequential heuristic. The PDF 372 across-stage sentence and the Issurin and endurance sentences are kept. |
| heuristic--sequential-accumulation-needs-4-6-week-stages-extensive-before-explosive.md | **Fix 6.** (1) "so, Inference: the 4-6 weeks is a minimum, not a tested optimum" and "Inference: Bondarchuk agrees on the direction". (2) After the Fig 5.18 sentence, the stage-level rule from PDF 300-301 is added with the "novices and athletes of average qualification" scope, checked against the page images. The Inference adds that "Fig 5.13 on PDF p. 300 labels the first-stage means 'Jumps'", so "speed-strength" there means jumping exercises, and the conflict turns on what the first stage contains. |
| claim--time-limits-of-single-emphasis-loading-by-motor-quality.md | **Fix 7.** "Unclear wording" is rewritten. Read literally, p.370 fits both p.372 session lists (quoted) but conflicts with the p.373 stage-level aerobic-first model. "Inference: if 'precedes' is a slip for 'is preceded by,' it fits p. 373 and not p. 372." Citations: "Both of p. 370's citations (Serafimova 1974; Naumenko 1978) appear among the four p. 373 gives for its aerobic-first warning (with Vavilov 1977 and Morzhevikov 1980)". |
| case-study--nedobyvailov-light-heavy-and-combined-loads-in-jumpers.md | **Fix 8.** Fig 6.25 values are now: absolute strength GP1 about 7, GP2 about 18, GP3 about 17; speed GP1 about 18, GP2 about 11, GP3 about 14; power GP1 about 6, GP2 about 14, GP3 about 20 ("the GP3 power bar ends on the 20 gridline"). The When NOT pair is now "about 17% ... about 18%". The Example reads "power rose about 20% ... against about 14% (70-90%) and about 6% (30-50%), while speed rose most, about 18%". |
| heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation.md | **Fix 9.** (1) "Inference: removing that disturbance too early removes part of the signal." (2) When NOT: "The text says training volume rose 'by an average of 15%' but not whether in both groups or only the restoration group (PDF p. 368); Inference: if only the restoration group, the result confounds restoration with extra volume." (3) A blank line is added before **Example**. (4) Beyond the review: the Example's "while also handling about 15% more volume" gave the volume rise to the restoration group too. It now quotes the sentence and adds "without saying in which group". |
| principle--loading-volume-disturbs-homeostasis-and-prepares-connective-tissue.md | **Missing idea 1.** After the PDF 370 intensification sentence, a short addition quotes the training-potential passage: "The training potential of the means employed decreases as the special work capacity increases" (Fig 6.28), and "it is inappropriate to use highly stimulating means prematurely, because the body is functionally unprepared for them ... disturbance of the natural course of adaptation" (PDF pp. 368-369, checked against the page images). Related annotates the existing 5.4.4 link and adds [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]]. |
| claim--middle-distance-runners-need-strength-and-jump-training-benchmarks.md | **Missing ideas 2 and 3.** A new paragraph says "The passage follows directly from the authors' rule for choosing SPP means". It quotes PDF 367 (external similarity "often overemphasized"; squats "justified"; means that "not only conform to, but exceed, competition conditions ... On this basis ... the strength component of the movement") and PDF 363, 6.8.3 ("cannot simply be used in a very general way"; running endurance and the rower or cyclist; "The emergence of specificity from an array of non-specific fitness qualities ... is not supported"). Both pages were checked against the page image. Related adds the 4.3.3 effort principle, the dynamic-correspondence heuristic and the specificity entry. The link notes that PDF 363's "discussed in 1.3" points to specificity, which is section 1.4 in this edition (PDF p. 38, text layer). That mismatch is labelled Inference. |

## Fig readings (my own, from 300 dpi renders)

- **Fig 6.30 (PDF 375 / p.364).** On the render, the month-1 tick is at about x 697 and month 2 at about 800; months 4 and 5 are at about 978 and 1065. The shaded block's left edge is at about 755, so about month 1.6. Its right edge is at about 1025, so about month 4.5. On the y axis, 4 is at y 457 and 6 at y 381, about 38 px per percentage point. Vertical jump peaks at about 7 near month 3.7 and ends at about 4.5-4.6 at month 8. Stride length peaks at about 11.5 near month 7 and ends at about 11. Ten jumps peaks at about 9.7 and ends at about 9.5. This agrees with the review. The entry keeps "about 11" and "about 9-9.5".
- **Fig 6.25 (PDF 365 / p.354).** On the y axis, 0 is at about y 462-465, 10 at about 351-354 and 20 at about 249-255, about 10.5 px per point. Absolute strength: GP1 about 7.0, GP2 about 18.0, GP3 about 16.7. Speed: GP1 about 18.0, GP2 about 11.2, GP3 about 13.6. Power: GP1 about 6.2, GP2 about 14.2, GP3 about 20.0 (on the gridline). This agrees with the review. The caption spells the name "Nedobyvailov".

## Missing ideas: placement

| # | idea | placement |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Do not use highly stimulating means prematurely (PDF 368-369) | Folded into 6c `principle--loading-volume-disturbs-homeostasis-and-prepares-connective-tissue`. Its title already says "Intensify Only After Extensive Low-Intensity Work", and Fig 6.28 sits on the same page as its 6.9.4 opening. The 5.4.4 `heuristic--replace-means-as-their-training-effect-fades` was already in Related. It covers replacing means but not the premature-use warning, so that link is now annotated. |
| 2 | SPP means must exceed competition conditions for highly qualified athletes (PDF 367) | Folded into 6c `claim--middle-distance-runners-need-strength-and-jump-training-benchmarks`. The PDF 367 passage leads straight into that entry's strength-for-endurance argument ("On this basis ... strength component"). The new angle, tying the rule to training potential and qualification, is not in 4.3.3. A Related link to [[principle--training-effort-must-match-or-exceed-sport-effort-judged-by-movement-speed]] (4.3.3) and the dynamic-correspondence heuristic was added. |
| 3 | 6.8.3: general qualities do not assemble into SPP (PDF 363) | Folded into the same middle-distance entry, as one sentence group. No Ch 1 entry carries the 6.8.3 statement. `principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions` (1.4) covers narrow transfer, and the 4.4 `principle--local-muscular-endurance-adaptation-is-specific-to-the-trained-muscles` (already in Related) holds the skier version of the running example. A link to the 1.4 entry was added. The review's "Ch1.3" is section 1.4 here: 1.3 is "A Philosophy of Physical Training" (PDF 35), and 1.4 is "Specificity in Training" (PDF 38). |

No new entry was written, so `_scope_supertraining_ch6c.txt` is unchanged (19 lines).

## Disagreements with the review

1. **Fix 5: the PDF 300 vs PDF 371 opposition is labelled Inference.** Neither page says barbell work is "strength" and jumping is "speed-strength". The review's rewrite stated the opposition as fact. The entry now says "Inference: reading barbell work as 'strength' and jumping as 'speed-strength' (Fig 5.13 on the same page labels the jumping means 'Jumps'), this opposes p. 371's 'preserve the above order'". Every other part of the review's rewrite held up on the page images.
2. **Fix 7: "the same ones" is loosened.** The review says the p.370 citations "are the same ones p. 373 gives". PDF 373 gives four (Naumenko 1978; Vavilov 1977; Serafimova 1974; Morzhevikov 1980), and p.370 gives two of them. The entry says "appear among the four".
3. **Fix 2, optional singular wording.** The review suggests "the athlete lost both". PDF 536 introduces Figure 8 "in triple jumpers" and then switches to "the athlete" and "his chance". The Example records both rather than picking one.
4. **Optional items not applied.** I did not add the PDF 438 / "Fig 1.7" note to the within-session entry, because I did not open PDF 438, and it would have been an unverified locator. I did not change the "page image not opened" note in the GO entry `framework--three-levels-of-change-in-fitness-state`, because it was outside the flagged files.

Every other review claim held up on the page: the Fig 6.30 block edges, the Fig 6.25 values, the PDF 515 title block, the PDF 536 reversal and its example, the PDF 300 heading that makes the PDF 301 bullets stage-level, the partial italics on PDF 371, Susman's placement on PDF 377, the PDF 368 15% sentence, and the PDF 305 4-12 weeks.

## Follow-up for the coordinator

- **Addendum voice (PDF 514-590) in other Supertraining entries.** I grepped the staging book folder, the whole staging library and the vault library for "PDF p(p). 5[1-9][0-9]", "536" and "Addendum". **No other entry attaches "the authors" to an Addendum statement.** One near miss: `heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next.md` is in both staging and the vault (the copies are identical). It cites PDF 536 as "the Addendum says ..." and labels it "text layer". The voice there is unlabelled rather than wrong. Recommend "Verkhoshansky's Addendum paper (9.1, translated by Yessis; PDF p. 515)" in both copies, and opening the page image. `_book.md` row 9 lists the Addendum, but it is a map, not an entry.

I applied all 9 fixes after checking each against the page. Three of the review's suggested wordings were looser than the source, so I changed them (listed under Disagreements below). I folded the 3 missing ideas into existing 6c entries, so there are no new entries and no renames. Every link resolves, and lint shows no issues in any 6c file.

The log is at `/Users/kristinarash/DEV/Flint/staging/fixes_supertraining_ch6c_applied.md`. Edited files are in `/Users/kristinarash/DEV/Flint/staging/library/strength-and-conditioning/supertraining--verkhoshansky/`: the 9 FIX entries plus 2 GO entries (for the missing ideas). The scope file still lists 19 entries. I did not touch `_book.md`, any 6b or 6d file, the vault, or git.

**Fix outcomes (all applied):**
1. **LDTE principle:** Fig 6.30 block is now about month 1.6 to 4.5. All three "4-12 weeks" uses are recorded with their pages (PDF 305, 375, and the Addendum on 536), with T2 ≈ T1 reconciling 375 and 536.
2. **Technique heuristic:** PDF 515 confirms the Addendum is "Dr. Yuri Verkhoshansky, Translated from the Russian by Dr. Michael Yessis". The entry now says "Verkhoshansky's Addendum paper" instead of "the authors". The translation-slip Inference is added, and the link to the 6d technique-work entry is in. It stays `contested`.
3. **Altitude claim:** the Susman sentence now uses the review's wording, with the reading labelled Inference.
4. **Concentrated claim:** now says "partly italicised", links the 6b framework and the 6d complex-training claim, and adds the optional scope Inference.
5. **Within-session heuristic:** the "contested" paragraph is rewritten. PDF 371 is called a hedge. The real conflict across chapters is laid out with PDF 288, 299 and 300. The PDF 301 bullets are moved out as stage-level rules.
6. **Sequential heuristic:** two Inference labels added, plus the PDF 300-301 stage-level rule.
7. **Time-limits claim:** the "Unclear wording" paragraph is re-sorted. The PDF 372 lists agree with the literal p.370 sentence; only p.373 conflicts with it.
8. **Nedobyvailov:** Fig 6.25 values corrected (below), along with the Example and the When NOT pair.
9. **Restoration heuristic:** two Inference labels and the missing blank line. Beyond the review, the Example also said the 15% volume rise was in the restoration group; it now says the text does not say which group.

**Disagreements with the review:**
- In fix 5, the review stated as fact that PDF 300's "strength followed by speed-strength" opposes p.371's "barbell then jumping". Neither page equates barbell with strength or jumping with speed-strength, so I labelled that link Inference (Fig 5.13 supports it).
- In fix 7, the review says p.370's citations are "the same ones" p.373 gives. p.373 gives four, and p.370's two are among them; the entry now says that.
- In fix 2, PDF 536 says "in triple jumpers" and then switches to "the athlete … his chance". I recorded both instead of picking singular or plural.
- I skipped the optional PDF 438 note because I didn't open that page.

**Figure readings** (300 dpi crops, measured against the gridlines):
- **Fig 6.30:** the month-1 tick is at about 697 px and month 2 at about 800. The shaded block runs from about 755 px (≈ month 1.6) to about 1025 px (≈ month 4.5). Vertical jump peaks at about 7 near month 3.7 and ends at about 4.5. Stride length peaks at about 11.5 and ends at about 11. Ten jumps peaks at about 9.7 and ends at about 9.5.
- **Fig 6.25** (≈10.5 px per point):

| | GP1 | GP2 | GP3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Absolute strength | about 7.0 | about 18.0 | about 16.7 |
| Speed | about 18.0 | about 11.2 | about 13.6 |
| Power | about 6.2 | about 14.2 | about 20.0 (on the gridline) |

Both agree with the review.

**Where the missing ideas went:**
1. The warning against using highly stimulating means too early (PDF 368-369) went into `principle--loading-volume-disturbs-homeostasis-and-prepares-connective-tissue`. Its 5.4.4 link is now annotated, and I linked the conjugate-sequence framework.
2. "SPP means must exceed competition conditions" (PDF 367) went into `claim--middle-distance-runners-need-strength-and-jump-training-benchmarks`, with links to the 4.3.3 effort principle and the dynamic-correspondence heuristic.
3. The 6.8.3 point that general qualities don't add up to special preparedness (PDF 363) went into the same claim, with a link to the specificity entry. The book's "discussed in 1.3" points to specificity, which is section 1.4 in this edition, so I noted that as Inference.

**Addendum follow-up:** no staged or vault Supertraining entry attaches "the authors" to an Addendum (PDF 514-590) statement. The one near miss is `heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next.md`, with identical copies in staging and the vault. It cites PDF 536 as "the Addendum says …" (text layer only), so the voice is unlabelled rather than wrong. I recommend changing it to "Verkhoshansky's Addendum paper" in both copies.

**Links:** all three 6b/6d targets existed when I linked them (13:51). The 6b framework had been modified at 13:40, so it was mid-edit; if the 6b fixer renames it, the link in the concentrated claim must follow. The reciprocal-link suggestions are in the log.
